Large mass self-similar solutions of the parabolic-parabolic Keller–Segel model of chemotaxis

Piotr Biler    Lucilla Corrias    Jean Dolbeault Affiliation: Instytut Matematyczny, Uniwersytet Wrocławski, pl. Grunwaldzki 2/4, 50–384 Wrocław, Poland. E-mail: Piotr.Biler@math.uni.wroc.pl Affiliation: Département de Mathématiques, Université d’Évry Val d’Essonne, rue du père Jarlan, F-91025 Évry Cédex, France. E-mail: lucilla.corrias@univ-evry.fr Affiliation: Ceremade (UMR CNRS 7534), Université Paris-Dauphine, Place de Lattre de Tassigny, F-75775 Paris Cédex 16, France. E-mail: dolbeaul@ceremade.dauphine.fr
August 24, 2026
Abstract

In two space dimensions, the parabolic-parabolic Keller–Segel system shares many properties with the parabolic-elliptic Keller–Segel system. In particular, solutions globally exist in both cases as long as their mass is less than 8​π8\,\pi. However, this threshold is not as clear in the parabolic-parabolic case as it is in the parabolic-elliptic case, in which solutions with mass above 8​π8\,\pi always blow up. Here we study forward self-similar solutions of the parabolic-parabolic Keller–Segel system and prove that, in some cases, such solutions globally exist even if their total mass is above 8​π8\,\pi, which is forbidden in the parabolic-elliptic case.

Keywords: 
Keller–Segel model chemotaxis self-similar solution nonlocal parabolic equations critical mass existence blowup

35B30 35K40 35K57 35J60

1 Introduction

The Keller–Segel model has been widely studied for almost forty years. It models the behavior of a slime mold of myxamoebae, Dictyostelium Discoideum, which have the peculiarity of organizing themselves to form aggregates by moving towards regions of a higher concentration of a chemoattractant. This chemoattractant, the cyclic adenosine monophosphate, is secreted by the amoebae themselves when they are lacking of nutrients. The Keller–Segel model is considered as a prototypical model for pattern formation in chemotaxis, and has attracted a lot of attention as a test case for more complex taxis phenomena driven by chemical substances. See [9, 10, 11, 17, 18] for further references.

The simplest version of the model is made of two equations, one for the density of the amoebae and another one for the density of the chemoattractant. Both are parabolic, although an even simpler version has been widely considered by neglecting the time-dependence of the density of the chemoattractant. We shall refer to the complete version of the model as the parabolic-parabolic model, and to the latter as the parabolic-elliptic Keller–Segel model.

The precise dependence of the diffusion coefficients and of the chemosensitivity parameter depends on the context. All variants of the model involve diffusions in the equations for the density of the amoebae and for the density of the chemoattractant. The coupling is due to the fact that amoebae move according to the gradient of the chemoattractant, and that the emission of the chemoattractant is proportional to the density of amoebae. A crude insight into the main features of the model can be gained from the simplest case, that is when the nonlinear term in the equation is quadratic, but more realistic models should probably involve more complex nonlinearities.

Since the slime mold usually moves over a planar substrate, it makes sense to consider two-dimensional geometries. In some cases, boundary effects are important, but they are out of the purpose of this paper and we shall therefore assume that the model is set on the two-dimensional Euclidean plane.

In the parabolic-elliptic model, there is a critical mass, 8​π8\,\pi after a proper adimensionalization, whose role is now rather well understood; see [8, 5]. Below such a mass, the diffusion predominates, in the sense that amoebae are unable to emit enough chemoattractant to aggregate. On large times, the population diffuses and locally vanishes, although the behavior significantly differs from a pure diffusion. Above 8​π8\,\pi, at least one singularity appears in finite time, which is interpreted as the occurrence of an aggregate.

Since singularities are local, it is widely believed that 8​π8\,\pi should also be a threshold between the diffusion dominated regime and the regime of aggregation also in the parabolic-parabolic model. This is certainly the case in some sense, for appropriate initial data, but the situation is not as simple as in the parabolic-elliptic case. It turns out that if, initially, the population of amoebae is scattered enough, and for a well chosen initial distribution of the chemoattractant, there are solutions for which the diffusion predominates for large times, even for masses larger than 8​π8\,\pi. It is the purpose of this paper to establish such a fact, for a special class of solutions and in a certain range of the parameters of the model.

In this paper, we consider the parabolic-parabolic Keller–Segel model

nt=Δn−∇⋅(n∇c),\displaystyle n_{t}=\Delta n-\nabla\cdot(n\,\nabla c)\,, (1)
τ​ct=Δ​c+n,\displaystyle\tau\,c_{t}=\Delta c+n\,, (2)

for the densities nn and cc of, respectively, microorganisms (e.g. amoebae) and diffusing chemicals that they are secreting. Interesting mathematical questions are related to qualitative properties of problem (1)–(2) such as global in time existence versus finite time blowup of solutions describing chemotactic concentration phenomena. After the pioneering works of Keller and Segel, a huge literature has dealt with the mathematical modelling of chemotaxis and its analysis. We recommend the reading of [9] for a recent review from both biological and mathematical points of view.

We shall consider the Keller–Segel system (1)–(2) for any t>0t>0, x∈ℝ2x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, supplemented with initial conditions n0n_{0} and c0c_{0}. From now on we shall assume that n0n_{0} and c0c_{0} are nonnegative and that n0n_{0} is integrable on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. As a consequence, for solutions with sufficiently fast decay at infinity, the total mass is conserved, i.e.,

M:=∫ℝ2n⁡(t,x)​𝑑x=∫ℝ2n0​(x)​𝑑xM:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}n(t,x)\,{\rm d}x=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}n_{0}(x)\,{\rm d}x

does not depend on tt.

Throughout the paper, τ\tau is a nonnegative parameter taking into account the difference of the time scales of the diffusive processes undergone by nn and cc. The qualitative properties of nn and cc (such as the asymptotic behavior for large values of tt) depend on τ\tau and the stability of system (1)–(2) with respect to τ\tau is expected, i.e. solutions of the parabolic-parabolic Keller–Segel system are expected to converge to those of parabolic-elliptic system when τ↘0\tau\searrow 0. This has been recently proved, at least for solutions with a suitably small mass MM, in [16]. Here, we are interested in the differences between the parabolic-elliptic Keller–Segel system (τ=0\tau=0) and the parabolic-parabolic Keller–Segel system (τ>0\tau>0). Known results are briefly summarized as follows.

When τ=0\tau=0 in (2), M=8​πM=8\,\pi is a threshold for existence versus blowup of the solution of (1)–(2), see [8, 5, 7]. Solutions globally exist for M<8​πM<8\,\pi, while explosion in finite time may occur if M>8​πM>8\,\pi. In the critical case M=8​πM=8\,\pi, the solutions are known to be global in time but the density grows and mass concentration occurs in infinite time; see [3, 4].

For τ>0\tau>0, according to [7], solutions globally exist for any M<8​πM<8\,\pi. However, it has not yet been proved that explosion occurs in finite time as soon as M>8​πM>8\,\pi, for instance under some additional assumptions like a smallness condition on ∫ℝ2|x|2​n0​(x)​𝑑x\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|x|^{2}\,n_{0}(x)\,{\rm d}x. If M=8​πM=8\,\pi, there is an infinite number of steady states (see [3]), but no other result is available, apart from self-similar solutions.

Motivated by this lack of results for (1)–(2), this paper deals with the existence of positive forward self-similar solutions of (1)–(2), i.e., solutions which can be written as

n⁡(t,x)=1t​u​(xt)andc⁡(t,x)=v⁡(xt),n(t,x)=\frac{1}{t}\,u\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{t}}\right)\quad\mbox{and}\quad c(t,x)=v\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{t}}\right), (3)

with a large total mass (that is, larger than 8​π8\,\pi). Indeed, since we are dealing with the two-dimensional case, any self-similar solution nn in L1​(ℝ2)L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) preserves mass, i.e., for each t≥0t\geq 0

∫ℝ2n⁡(t,x)​𝑑x=∫ℝ2u⁡(ξ)​𝑑ξ=M.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}n(t,x)\,{\rm d}x=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}u(\xi)\,{\rm d}\xi=M\,.

Therefore, for any given τ>0\tau>0, we are interested in the optimal range of MM for the existence of such solutions, and in uniqueness or multiplicity issues for a given MM in the optimal range. Actually, our goal is double. The main one is to prove the above mentioned existence result. Second, we will give an as complete as possible review of the numerous existing results on the topic and also simplified, new proofs of them. For this reason, the remainder of the introduction will be primarily devoted to the state of the art on self-similar solutions.

Self-similar solutions can be obtained through various approaches. The first method for the study of self-similar solutions (see for example [1] and the references therein) amounts to look for mild solutions of (1)–(2), that is, solutions of

n(t,⋅)=e(t−t0)​Δn(t0,⋅)−∫t0t(∇e(t−s)​Δ)⋅(n(s,⋅)∇c(s,⋅))ds,\displaystyle n(t,\cdot)={\rm e}^{(t-t_{0})\Delta}\,n(t_{0},\cdot)-\int_{t_{0}}^{t}\left(\nabla{\rm e}^{(t-s)\Delta}\right)\cdot\big(n(s,\cdot)\,\nabla c(s,\cdot)\big)\,{\rm d}s\,,
c⁡(t,⋅)=et−t0τ​Δ​c​(t0,⋅)+1τ​∫t0tet−sτ​Δ​n​(s,⋅)​𝑑s,\displaystyle c(t,\cdot)={\rm e}^{\frac{t-t_{0}}{\tau}\Delta}\,c(t_{0},\cdot)+\frac{1}{\tau}\int_{t_{0}}^{t}{\rm e}^{\frac{t-s}{\tau}\Delta}\,n(s,\cdot)\,{\rm d}s\,,

for any t>t0≥0t>t_{0}\geq 0. Roughly speaking, such self-similar solutions are obtained by a fixed point theorem. However, smallness conditions on the initial data are required in order to apply a contraction mapping principle; see [14], where this method has been applied to (1)–(2) with τ=1\tau=1. Therefore, covering the whole range of masses for which solutions exists seems out of reach in this setting.

Alternatively, one can prove the existence of self-similar solutions through the direct analysis of the elliptic system satisfied by (u,v)(u,v), i.e.,

Δu−∇⋅(u∇v−12ξu)=0,\displaystyle\Delta u-\nabla\cdot\left(u\,\nabla v-\frac{1}{2}\,\xi\,u\right)=0\,, (4)
Δ​v+τ2​ξ⋅∇v+u=0,\displaystyle\Delta v+\frac{\tau}{2}\,\xi\cdot\nabla v+u=0\,, (5)

where ξ=x/t\xi=x/\sqrt{t} and the differential operators in (4)–(5) are taken with respect to ξ\xi. In this case, a natural functional space to be considered for both uu and vv is the subspace C02​(ℝ2)C^{2}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) of functions in the space C2​(ℝ2)C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) such that

lim|ξ|→∞u⁡(ξ)=0andlim|ξ|→∞v⁡(ξ)=0.\lim_{|\xi|\to\infty}u(\xi)=0\quad\mbox{and}\quad\lim_{|\xi|\to\infty}v(\xi)=0\,.

For such classical solutions, equation (4) can be written equivalently as either

∇⋅[u∇(logu−v+|ξ|24)]=0,\nabla\cdot\left[u\,\nabla\left(\log u-v+\frac{|\xi|^{2}}{4}\right)\right]=0\,,

or

∇⋅[eve−|ξ|2/4∇(ue−ve|ξ|2/4)]=0.\nabla\cdot\left[{\rm e}^{v}\,{\rm e}^{-|\xi|^{2}/4}\,\nabla\left(u\,{\rm e}^{-v}\,{\rm e}^{|\xi|^{2}/4}\right)\right]=0\,.

Then, using the fact that uu, vv, and consequently |∇v||\nabla v| are bounded, it has been proved in [15] that there exists a constant σ\sigma such that

u⁡(ξ)=σ​ev⁡(ξ)​e−|ξ|24u(\xi)=\sigma\,{\rm e}^{v(\xi)}{\rm e}^{-\frac{|\xi|^{2}}{4}} (6)

for any ξ∈ℝ2\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. Since uu is positive by the maximum principle, it follows that σ\sigma is positive. As a consequence, u∈L1​(ℝ2)u\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), and the stationary system (4)–(5) reduces to a family of nonlinear elliptic equations for vv, namely

Δ​v+τ2​ξ⋅∇v+σ​ev​e−|ξ|24=0,\Delta v+\frac{\tau}{2}\,\xi\cdot\nabla v+\sigma\,{\rm e}^{v}\,{\rm e}^{-\frac{|\xi|^{2}}{4}}=0\,, (7)

v⁡(ξ)≤C​e−min⁡{1,τ}​|ξ|24,v(\xi)\leq C\,{\rm e}^{-\min\{1,\tau\}\frac{|\xi|^{2}}{4}}, (8)

where CC is any positive constant such that C​min⁡{1,τ}≥σ​e‖v‖∞C\min\{1,\tau\}\geq\sigma\,{\rm e}^{\|v\|_{\infty}}; see for instance [15]. Therefore, v∈L1​(ℝ2)v\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) holds true for any solution of (7) in C02​(ℝ2)C^{2}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{2}).

The range of MM for which self-similar solutions exist in C02​(ℝ2)C^{2}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) gives an indication on the range of MM for which some solutions of (1)–(2) may globally exist. Self-similar solutions indeed provide explicit examples of global solutions, even with smooth initial data, up to a time-shift: take for instance uu and vv as the initial data for (1)–(2). Moreover, if self-similar solutions describe the asymptotic behavior of any solution of (1)–(2) under appropriate conditions on initial data, then the ranges of global existence of solutions should be exactly the same. This property has been established in [5] for τ=0\tau=0. In the case τ>0\tau>0, this might not be as simple as in the case τ=0\tau=0 if one can prove that blowup may occur for any M>8​πM>8\,\pi. However, at least for initial data close enough to uu and vv, one can expect that the ranges of global existence are the same.

In view of our main goal, we are actually more interested in parametrizing the set of C02​(ℝ2)C^{2}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) self-similar solutions in terms of mass rather than in terms of σ\sigma. This is possible using in (7) the relation

M=σ​∫ℝ2ev⁡(ξ)​e−|ξ|24​𝑑ξ.M=\sigma\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}{\rm e}^{v(\xi)}\,{\rm e}^{-\frac{|\xi|^{2}}{4}}\,{\rm d}\xi\,. (9)

However, by doing that, equation (7) becomes nonlocal, as was the original system (1)–(2), and the problem is definitely more difficult to handle. Another not less important reason to consider a different but equivalent formulation of problem (4)–(5) is that the correspondence between σ\sigma and MM is not clear due to the lack of uniqueness of solutions to (7); see Remark 1 at the end of Section 2.

For the sake of completeness, we have to say that equation (7), written as

has been studied using variational methods in [13, 19]. The weighted functional space H1​(ℝ2,exp⁡(τ4​|ξ|2)​d​ξ)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\exp(\frac{\tau}{4}|\xi|^{2})\,{\rm d}\xi) is then natural, but working in this space introduces a condition on the values of τ\tau, which have to be in the interval (0,2)(0,2). Under such a restriction, it has been established that solutions exist if 0<σ<σ∗0<\sigma<\sigma^{*}, for some σ∗>0\sigma^{*}>0. These solutions are positive and belong to C02​(ℝ2)C^{2}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), but due to the restriction on τ\tau, one has to look for alternative approaches.

Another important and useful result has been obtained in [15] using the moving planes technique: any positive solution v∈C02​(ℝ2)v\in C^{2}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) of (7) must be radially symmetric. As a consequence, system (4)–(5) reduces to the ODE system

u(r)=σev⁡(r)e−r2/4,\displaystyle u(r)=\sigma\,{\rm e}^{v(r)}\,{\rm e}^{-r^{2}/4},

Being this the state of the art, we will establish that the formulation of system (10)–(11) in terms of cumulated densities is better adapted to the qualitative description of uu and vv. This is a classical technique used previously, for example, in the context of the parabolic-elliptic Keller–Segel system and astrophysical models; see [1, 3] and further references therein. For τ>0\tau>0, many qualitative properties of the solutions can still be proved in this framework. These will allow us to build positive forward self-similar solutions of (1)–(2) satisfying (3), which have an arbitrarily large mass when τ\tau is large enough. The obtained results are summarized in the theorem below. One may interpret it by saying that the diffusion of cc described by (2) for positive large τ\tau and some M>8​πM>8\,\pi may prevent the blowup of the solutions of the parabolic-parabolic Keller–Segel system. This is a major difference with the parabolic-elliptic case τ=0\tau=0, for which the response of cc to the variations of nn being instantaneous, any smooth solution with mass M>8​πM>8\,\pi must concentrate and blow up in finite time.

Theorem 1.1

For any M>0M>0, there exists some τ~​(M)≥0\tilde{\tau}(M)\geq 0 such that for any τ≥τ~​(M)\tau\geq\tilde{\tau}(M) there is at least one solution (u,v)(u,v) of (4)–(5) in (C02​(ℝ2))2(C^{2}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))^{2} with u>0u>0 of mass MM and v>0v>0. If M<8​πM<8\,\pi, τ~​(M)=0\tilde{\tau}(M)=0. If M>8​πM>8\,\pi, τ~​(M)\tilde{\tau}(M) is positive and there are at least two solutions, except for the maximal possible value of MM. All solutions are radial, nonincreasing, with fast decay at infinity, and hence attain their maximum at x=0x=0. They are uniquely determined by a:=u⁡(0)/2a:=u(0)/2, which in turn uniquely determines M=M⁡(a,τ)M=M(a,\tau). Moreover, lima→∞M⁡(a,τ)=8​π\lim_{a\to\infty}M(a,\tau)=8\,\pi, while, as a→∞a\to\infty, the corresponding solution uu concentrates into a Dirac delta distribution, up to the factor 8​π8\,\pi, and v⁡(0)=‖v‖L∞​(ℝ2)v(0)=\|v\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2})} becomes arbitrarily large.

This paper is organized as follows. We shall first establish the main a priori estimates for Theorem 1.1 in the next section. The framework of cumulated densities is developed in Section 3, which also contains more detailed statements than the ones of Theorem 1.1. The remaining a priori estimates and proofs are given in Sections 4 and 5, respectively. Section 6 is devoted to some numerical results and Section 7 to concluding remarks.

2 Large mass positive forward self-similar solutions

Before restating the question of self-similar solutions in terms of cumulated densities, let us establish the key a priori estimate for Theorem 1.1, which proves that these solutions may have an arbitrary large mass when τ\tau is large enough. This result is entirely new. Such an estimate can be obtained both from equation (12) and from the cumulated densities formulation. In this section, we shall establish this a priori estimate in the first setting. It will be translated in the cumulated densities framework in Section 4.

From now on, we shall parametrize MM in term of aa and τ\tau, i.e. M=M⁡(a,τ)M=M(a,\tau), where a=u⁡(0)/2a=u(0)/2 will be the shooting parameter in the cumulated densities shooting problem, see (29)–(30) and (33)–(34) below.

Remark 1

Estimates (25) on σ\sigma are new. The authors of [15] analyzed the map s↦σ⁡(s)s\mapsto\sigma(s), where ss is the shooting parameter defined in (16), and they proved that it is a continuous map from ℝ\mathbb{R} into ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} with lims→±∞σ⁡(s)=0\lim_{s\to\pm\infty}\sigma(s)=0. Therefore, σ\sigma must be bounded for any fixed τ\tau by σ∗=σ⁡(s∗)\sigma^{*}=\sigma(s^{*}), for some s∗∈ℝs^{*}\in\mathbb{R}, and problem (12)–(14) admits no solution for σ>σ∗\sigma>\sigma^{*}, at least one solution for σ=σ∗\sigma=\sigma^{*} and finally (at least) two distinct solutions for 0<σ<σ∗0<\sigma<\sigma^{*}. However, estimates on σ\sigma (or σ∗\sigma^{*}) were missing.

Remark 2

Estimate (20) says that, for any fixed σ>0\sigma>0 and τ>0\tau>0, v⁡(0)v(0) satisfies

v⁡(0)−σ​I​(τ)​ev⁡(0)≤0.v(0)-\,\sigma\,I(\tau)\,{\rm e}^{v(0)}\leq 0\,.

Since the function x↦x−σ​I​(τ)​exx\,\mapsto\,x-\sigma\,I(\tau)\,{\rm e}^{x} is strictly concave and attains the maximum in x=−log⁡(σ​I​(τ))x=-\log(\sigma\,I(\tau)), we deduce that whenever σ​I​(τ)<1/e\sigma\,I(\tau)<1/{\rm e}, there exists an open interval J⊂ℝ+J\subset\mathbb{R}_{+} of non existence of solutions of (12) satisfying (14), with v⁡(0)∈Jv(0)\in J. On the other hand if σ​I​(τ)≥1/e\sigma\,I(\tau)\geq 1/{\rm e}, the above inequality induces no restriction on v⁡(0)v(0).

3 Cumulated densities and main results

Let us introduce the cumulated densities formulation of the parabolic-parabolic Keller–Segel model as in [1], in terms of the functions uu and vv which solve problem (10)–(11), by defining

ϕ⁡(y):=12​π​∫B⁡(0,y)u⁡(ξ)​𝑑ξ=∫0yr​u​(r)​𝑑r,\displaystyle\phi(y):=\frac{1}{2\,\pi}\int_{B(0,\sqrt{y})}u(\xi)\,{\rm d}\xi=\int_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}r\,u(r)\,{\rm d}r\,,
ψ⁡(y):=12​π​∫B⁡(0,y)v⁡(ξ)​𝑑ξ=∫0yr​v​(r)​𝑑r.\displaystyle\psi(y):=\frac{1}{2\,\pi}\int_{B(0,\sqrt{y})}v(\xi)\,{\rm d}\xi=\int_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}r\,v(r)\,{\rm d}r\,.

Using the relations

ϕ′​(y)=12​u​(y)andϕ′′​(y)=14​y​u′​(y),\displaystyle\phi^{\prime}(y)=\frac{1}{2}\,u\left(\sqrt{y}\right)\quad\mbox{and}\quad\phi^{\prime\prime}(y)=\frac{1}{4\,\sqrt{y}}\,u^{\prime}\left(\sqrt{y}\right)\,, (26)
ψ′​(y)=12​v​(y)andψ′′​(y)=14​y​v′​(y),\displaystyle\psi^{\prime}(y)=\frac{1}{2}\,v\left(\sqrt{y}\right)\quad\mbox{and}\quad\psi^{\prime\prime}(y)=\frac{1}{4\,\sqrt{y}}\,v^{\prime}\left(\sqrt{y}\right)\,,

it follows from (10)–(11) that the cumulated densities ϕ\phi and ψ\psi solve the second order ODE system

ϕ′′+14​ϕ′−2​ϕ′​ψ′′=0,\displaystyle\phi^{\prime\prime}+\frac{1}{4}\,\phi^{\prime}-2\,\phi^{\prime}\psi^{\prime\prime}=0\,, (27)
4​y​ψ′′+τ​y​ψ′−τ​ψ+ϕ=0,\displaystyle 4\,y\,\psi^{\prime\prime}+\tau\,y\,\psi^{\prime}-\tau\,\psi+\phi=0\,, (28)

where (11) has been multiplied by rr and integrated on (0,y)(0,\sqrt{y}). Observing that equation (28) can be written as

4​(y​ψ′−ψ)′+τ⁡(y​ψ′−ψ)+ϕ=0,4\,(y\,\psi^{\prime}-\psi)^{\prime}+\tau\,(y\,\psi^{\prime}-\psi)+\phi=0\,,

and defining S⁡(y):=4​(ψ⁡(y)−y​ψ′​(y))′=−4​y​ψ′′​(y)=−y​v′​(y)S(y):=4\,(\psi(y)-y\,\psi^{\prime}(y))^{\prime}=-4\,y\,\psi^{\prime\prime}(y)=-{\sqrt{y}}\,v^{\prime}(\sqrt{y}) as in [2, 15], system (27)–(28) becomes, after a differentiation of (28) with respect to yy, a first order system in the (ϕ′,S)(\phi^{\prime},S) variables

ϕ′′+14​ϕ′+12​y​ϕ′​S=0,\displaystyle\phi^{\prime\prime}+\frac{1}{4}\,\phi^{\prime}+\frac{1}{2\,y}\,\phi^{\prime}S=0\,, (29)
S′+τ4​S=ϕ′.\displaystyle S^{\prime}+\frac{\tau}{4}\,S=\phi^{\prime}\,. (30)

The last formulation of the ODE system can be equivalently written as a single integro-differential equation, hence nonlocal, for ϕ′\phi^{\prime},

ϕ′′+14ϕ′+12​yϕ′e−τy/4∫0yeτ​z/4ϕ′(z)dz=0,\phi^{\prime\prime}+\frac{1}{4}\,\phi^{\prime}+\frac{1}{2\,y}\,\phi^{\prime}\,{\rm e}^{-\tau\,y/4}\int_{0}^{y}{\rm e}^{\tau\,z/4}\,\phi^{\prime}(z)\,{\rm d}z=0\,, (31)

since, by (30),

S(y)=e−τy/4∫0yeτ​z/4ϕ′(z)dz,S(y)={\rm e}^{-\tau\,y/4}\int_{0}^{y}{\rm e}^{\tau\,z/4}\,\phi^{\prime}(z)\,{\rm d}z\,, (32)

and as a single, local but nonlinear second order ODE for SS,

S′′+14​(τ+1)​S′+τ16​S+12​y​(S​S′+τ4​S2)=0,S^{\prime\prime}+\frac{1}{4}\,(\tau+1)\,S^{\prime}+\frac{\tau}{16}\,S+\frac{1}{2\,y}\left(S\,S^{\prime}+\frac{\tau}{4}\,S^{2}\right)=0\,,

which is obtained by differentiating (30). We will use in the sequel all these formulations in order to get a priori estimates.

For any positive self-similar solution (u,v)∈(C02​(ℝ2))2(u,v)\in(C^{2}_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{2}))^{2}, the natural initial conditions for (29)–(30) are

ϕ(0)=0,ϕ′(0)=a>0andS(0)=0,\phi(0)=0\,,\quad\phi^{\prime}(0)=a>0\quad\mbox{and}\quad S(0)=0\,, (33)

in view of the definition of ϕ\phi and of (32). Moreover, for any self-similar solution u∈L1​(ℝ2)u\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}), the corresponding cumulated density ϕ\phi satisfies the boundary condition

ϕ⁡(∞):=limy→∞ϕ⁡(y)=M⁡(a,τ)2​π.\phi(\infty):=\lim_{y\to\infty}\phi(y)=\frac{M(a,\tau)}{2\,\pi}\,. (34)

The problem is now formulated in terms of a shooting parameter problem (29)–(30), (33), with a new shooting parameter aa which is directly related to the concentration of the self-similar density uu around the origin, since a=u⁡(0)/2a=u(0)/2. This has been obtained in Section 2 and will be made more precise below. Let us observe that the relation between aa and the shooting parameter ss defined in (16) is 2​a=es2\,a={\rm e}^{s}, since s=v⁡(0)+log⁡σs=v(0)+\log\sigma. Thus, a one-to-one relation is established between the initial valued problems (29)–(30), (33) and (15)–(16) as soon as an existence and uniqueness result is established for one of them. Moreover, we have

v⁡(0)=v⁡(y)+12​∫0yS⁡(z)z​𝑑z,v(0)=v(\sqrt{y})+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{y}\frac{S(z)}{z}\,{\rm d}z\,,

and the boundary condition limr→∞v⁡(r)=0\lim_{r\to\infty}v(r)=0 is equivalent to

v⁡(0)=12​∫0∞S⁡(z)z​𝑑z.v(0)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{S(z)}{z}\,{\rm d}z\,. (35)

We also have: σ=limr→∞u⁡(r)​er2/4=2​limy→∞ϕ′​(y)​ey/4\sigma=\lim_{r\to\infty}u(r)\,{\rm e}^{{r^{2}}/{4}}=2\lim_{y\to\infty}\phi^{\prime}(y)\;{\rm e}^{\,y/4}. Hence we can reparametrize v⁡(0)v(0) and σ\sigma in terms of aa and τ\tau.

The main statements we are going to prove are summarized in the following theorems. The a priori estimates will be established in Section 4. The proofs will be given in Section 5. We shall say that (ϕ,S)(\phi,S) is a positive solution if both ϕ\phi and SS are positive functions.

For any fixed τ>0\tau>0 there exists M∗=M∗​(τ)≥8​πM^{*}=M^{*}(\tau)\geq 8\,\pi such that problem (29)–(30) with the boundary conditions

The estimate τ∗>1/2\tau^{*}>1/2 will be given in Proposition 1, as well as refined estimates on M⁡(a,τ)M(a,\tau). Theoretical results show that τ∗∈(0.5,16.1109​…)\tau^{*}\in(0.5,16.1109\ldots), see Th. 37, (36)–(37) and Sec. 2, while numerical computations suggests that τ∗∈(0.62,0.64)\tau^{*}\in(0.62,0.64), see Fig. 2 (right). This is a significant difference with the monotone dependence of self-similar solutions of the parabolic-elliptic Keller–Segel system (see (3, Sec. 4)).

4 Qualitative properties of ϕ\phi and SS

In the present section we will derive all a priori estimates on ϕ\phi and SS which are necessary to prove Theorems 37, 3.2 and 3.3. Some of them are new while other were already known. In any case, we shall give a unified and simplified proof of all of them in terms of cumulated densities.

5.3 Proof of Theorem 3.3

For any fixed τ\tau, let us define M∗​(τ)=supa>0M⁡(a,τ)M^{*}(\tau)=\sup_{a>0}M(a,\tau). Since MM is bounded from above with respect to τ\tau, uniformly in aa, continuous with respect to aa, such that M⁡(0,τ)=0M(0,\tau)=0 and lima→∞M⁡(a,τ)→8​π\lim_{a\to\infty}M(a,\tau)\to 8\,\pi, M∗​(τ)M^{*}(\tau) is well defined and finite. The theorem is then a straightforward consequence of Theorem 37 and Proposition 1. ∎

6 Numerical results

In this section, we numerically illustrate the above results. In particular, we show the existence of positive forward self-similar solutions with mass above 8​π8\,\pi and their multiplicity when τ\tau is large enough. We follow two different approaches: first the formulation (15)–(16), and then the cumulated densities formulation based on (29)–(30).

6.1 Bifurcation diagrams

The computations giving rise to Figs. 1 and 2 are based on the parametrization provided by (15)–(16). Numerically, one has to be careful with the origin and solve (15) on the interval (ε,∞)(\varepsilon,\infty) with the initial conditions

w⁡(ε,s)=s−14​ε2​esandw′​(ε,s)=−12​ε​es,w(\varepsilon\,;s)=s-\frac{1}{4}\,\varepsilon^{2}\,{\rm e}^{s}\quad\mbox{and}\quad w^{\prime}(\varepsilon\,;s)=-\frac{1}{2}\,\varepsilon\,{\rm e}^{s}\,,

obtained by the Taylor expansion at ε>0\varepsilon>0, small enough, thus dropping higher order terms in ε\varepsilon. Observe that by (15) w′′(0;s)=−es/2w^{\prime\prime}(0\,;s)=-{\rm e}^{s}/2. In case of Fig. 2, one has to compute M⁡(s)M(s), which is given by (17), by solving M′(r)=2πew⁡(r,s)e−r2/4rM^{\prime}(r)=2\,\pi\,{\rm e}^{w(r;s)}\,{\rm e}^{-r^{2}/4}\,r with the approximate initial condition M⁡(ε)=π​ε2​esM(\varepsilon)=\pi\,\varepsilon^{2}\,{\rm e}^{s}.

In Fig. 2, we recover that M⁡(s)→8​πM(s)\to 8\,\pi as s→∞s\to\infty. Moreover, for τ\tau large enough, there are two solutions corresponding to a given MM larger than 8​π8\,\pi, with M−8​πM-8\,\pi not too large. Since it is of interest to decide for which values of τ\tau solutions may have mass larger than 8​π8\,\pi, the small rectangle in Fig. 2 (left) is enlarged in Fig. 2 (right).

It can be numerically checked that solving the equations on (ε,rmax)(\varepsilon,r_{\rm max}) with rmax=10r_{\rm max}\!=\!10 gives a good approximation of the solution. Furthermore, here we took ε=10−8\varepsilon=10^{-8} and s∈[−10,20]s\in[-10,20].

Plots and bifurcation diagrams of forward self-similar solutions can be computed in the framework of cumulated densities (29)–(30), (33). However, again one has to be careful with the singularity at the origin. As above, since for ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough, S′∼ϕ′∼aS^{\prime}\sim\phi^{\prime}\sim a on (0,ε)(0,\varepsilon) and so

for any y∈(0,ε)y\in(0,\varepsilon). Obviously, having fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0, one has to take aa in such a way that ϕ′​(ε)−a=o⁡(a)\phi^{\prime}(\varepsilon)-a=o(a). Here, we choose ε=10−6\varepsilon=10^{-6}. Finally, we shall approximate MM from below by ϕ⁡(ymax)\phi(y_{\rm max}) with ymaxy_{\rm max} large enough. Figs. 3 and 4 correspond to the cases τ=0.1\tau=0.1 and τ=10\tau=10 respectively. For τ=0.1\tau=0.1, the value 8​π8\,\pi for the total mass is achieved only asymptotically in the limit a→∞a\to\infty. For τ=10\tau=10, self-similar solutions with mass MM larger than 8​π8\,\pi exist for aa large enough. Finally, Figs. 5 and 6 show the total mass as a function of aa and τ\tau.

7 Conclusions

Self-similar solutions are much more than an example of a family of solutions. The experience of various nonlinear diffusion equations shows that they are likely to be attracting a whole class of solutions, although this is still an open question for the parabolic-parabolic Keller–Segel model with large mass (see [14] for a result for small mass solutions). It is quite reasonable to expect that well chosen perturbations of these solutions asymptotically converge in self-similar variables to the stationary solutions we have found. This actually raises a much more interesting question, which is how to determine the basin of attraction of these self-similar solutions and to understand where is the threshold between solutions for which diffusion predominates and solutions which aggregate. Clearly, it is not going to be as simple as in the parabolic-elliptic case, where a single parameter, the total mass, determines the asymptotic regime. We can conjecture that blowup occurs for mass large enough and even, maybe, as soon as the total mass of the system is above 8​π8\,\pi if initial data are sufficiently concentrated.

The model considered in this paper is by many aspects ridiculously simple. See, for instance, [9] to get a taste of the variety of the nonlinearities that make sense even for a rather crude modelling purpose. Still, these models, in limiting regimes, asymptotically exhibit scaling properties similar to the ones of the parabolic-parabolic Keller–Segel model considered here. Therefore, we believe that the information gathered above, together with the methods that have been introduced, for instance, the cumulated densities reformulation of the model, should definitely be some valuable piece of information in the study of the asymptotic behaviors of the equations used in chemotaxis.
